title: Biodiversity and its Conservation
syllabus: Concept of Biodiversity (Genetic, Species, Ecological diversity); Patterns of Biodiversity (Latitudinal gradients, Species-Area relationships); Importance of Biodiversity (David Tilman's experiments, Paul Ehrlich's Rivet Popper hypothesis); Loss of Biodiversity ('The Evil Quartet' - Habitat loss and fragmentation, Over-exploitation, Alien species invasions, Co-extinctions); Biodiversity Conservation (Narrowly utilitarian, Broadly utilitarian, Ethical reasons); In-situ Conservation (Biosphere reserves, National parks, Wildlife sanctuaries, Sacred groves, Biodiversity hotspots) and Ex-situ Conservation (Zoological parks, Botanical gardens, Wildlife safari parks, Cryopreservation, Seed banks, Tissue culture); Endangered organisms, IUCN Red List / Red Data Book; International Conventions (Earth Summit and World Summit).

questions.question: The term 'Biodiversity' was popularised by which sociobiologist to describe the combined diversity at all levels of biological organization?
questions.solution: Sociobiologist Edward Wilson popularised the term 'biodiversity' to describe the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation—from macromolecules within cells to biomes.

questions.question: The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges shows variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine. This is an example of:
questions.solution: Genetic diversity is the diversity of genes within a species. The genetic variation shown by Rauwolfia vomitoria in terms of potency and concentration of the chemical reserpine across Himalayan ranges illustrates genetic diversity.

questions.question: The Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats. This represents which level of biological diversity?
questions.solution: Species diversity refers to the variety of species within a region. For example, the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.

questions.question: According to Robert May's global estimates, the total number of species existing on Earth is approximately:
questions.solution: Robert May placed the global species diversity at a scientifically sound estimate of about 7 million species. (The number of currently named and described species is slightly more than 1.5 million according to IUCN 2004).

questions.question: Among all recorded animal species on Earth, which taxonomic group is the most species-rich, making up more than 70 percent of all animals?
questions.solution: Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total. That means, out of every 10 animals on this planet, 7 are insects.

questions.question: Although India has only 2.4 percent of the world's land area, its share of the global species diversity is an impressive ________, making it one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world:
questions.solution: India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, but its share of the global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent. This makes India one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world.

questions.question: In general, species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles. Which of the following is NOT a hypothesized reason for the greater biodiversity in the tropics?
options: Tropical latitudes have experienced frequent glaciations in the past that promoted mass speciation.
Tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively more constant, and predictable, promoting niche specialization.
More solar energy is available in the tropics, contributing to higher productivity.
Tropical communities have had more evolutionary time to diversify without frequent glaciations.
questions.solution: Unlike temperate regions subjected to frequent glaciations in the past, tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years and thus had a long evolutionary time along with constant, predictable climates and higher solar energy for speciation.

questions.question: The great Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on Earth. It is estimated to harbor at least how many species of plants, fishes, birds, and mammals respectively?
questions.solution: Amazonian rainforest is home to more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles, and more than 125,000 invertebrates.

questions.question: German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit. On a logarithmic scale, this relationship is a straight line described by the equation:
questions.solution: On a logarithmic scale, the species-area relationship is linear: $\log S = \log C + Z \log A$, where $S = \text{Species richness}$, $A = \text{Area}$, $Z = \text{slope of the line (regression coefficient)}$, and $C = Y\text{-intercept}$.

questions.question: For small or moderately sized areas, the value of the regression coefficient ($Z$) in species-area relationships lies in the range of 0.1 to 0.2. However, for very large areas like entire continents (e.g., frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests), the slope ($Z$) is much steeper and ranges between:
options: 0.6 to 1.2 (specifically 1.15 for frugivorous birds and mammals)
questions.solution: When analyzing species-area relationships across very large areas like entire continents, the slope of the line ($Z$ value) is much steeper, ranging from 0.6 to 1.2 (for frugivorous birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, the slope is found to be 1.15).

questions.question: Long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots conducted by David Tilman showed that:
options: Plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and increased diversity contributed to higher productivity
Plots with fewer species had higher stability and greater productivity
Species diversity had no impact on ecosystem stability
Biomass fluctuations were highest in plots with the highest species richness
questions.solution: David Tilman's long-term outdoor plot experiments demonstrated that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass. He also showed that increased diversity contributed to higher overall community productivity.

questions.question: In the 'Rivet Popper hypothesis' proposed by Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich, the popping of rivets on the airplane wings represents:
options: The extinction of a key species that drives major ecosystem functions
The loss of an endangered bird species in a zoo
The introduction of an exotic weed species
questions.solution: In Paul Ehrlich's analogy: the airplane = ecosystem; rivets = species; popping a rivet = causing a species to become extinct. Loss of rivets on the wings (key species driving major ecosystem functions) poses a direct and serious threat to flight safety (ecosystem stability).

questions.question: According to the IUCN Red List (2004), how many total species (including vertebrates, invertebrates, and plants) have become extinct in the last 500 years?
questions.solution: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species in the last 500 years, including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, and 87 plants.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding recently extinct animal species and their native geographical countries:

List-I (Extinct Species)List-II (Country of Origin)
(A) Dodo(I) Australia
(B) Quagga(II) Mauritius
(C) Thylacine(III) Africa
(D) Steller's Sea Cow(IV) Russia

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Dodo: Mauritius; Quagga: Africa; Thylacine (marsupial wolf): Australia; Steller's Sea Cow: Russia; Three tiger subspecies (Bali, Javan, Caspian) are also recently extinct.

questions.question: The three subspecies of tiger that have become extinct in recent times are:
questions.solution: The three recent extinct subspecies of tiger (Panthera tigris) are Bali, Javan, and Caspian.

questions.question: The ongoing 'Sixth Extinction' episode on Earth is different from the previous five mass extinction episodes because the current rate of extinction is:
options: 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and is driven primarily by anthropogenic activities
10 times slower than pre-human background rates
Caused solely by volcanic eruptions and meteor strikes
questions.solution: The current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and human activities are responsible for these accelerated rates of biodiversity loss.

questions.question: 'The Evil Quartet' is the sobriquet used to describe the four major causes of biodiversity losses. The MOST IMPORTANT of these causes driving animals and plants to extinction is:
questions.solution: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction. Once covering more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface, tropical rainforests now cover no more than 6 per cent.

questions.question: The Amazon rain forest, often called the 'lungs of the planet', is being cut and cleared primarily for:
options: Cultivating soybeans and converting into grasslands for raising beef cattle
questions.solution: The Amazon rainforest is being cut and cleared for cultivating soya beans or for conversion to grasslands for raising beef cattle.

questions.question: Extinction of the Passenger Pigeon and Steller's Sea Cow in the last 500 years was driven primarily by which anthropogenic factor?
options: Over-exploitation by humans for food and resources
questions.solution: Humans have always depended on nature for food and shelter, but when 'need' turns to 'greed', it leads to over-exploitation. Many species extinctions in the last 500 years (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon) were due to over-exploitation by humans.

questions.question: The introduction of the Nile perch into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to the environmental disaster of:
options: The extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake
The rapid proliferation of water hyacinth
The poisoning of native African catfishes
Severe eutrophication due to toxic algal blooms
questions.solution: When alien species are introduced unintentionally or deliberately, some of them turn invasive and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species. The introduction of the Nile perch into Lake Victoria led to the extinction of over 200 species of native cichlid fish.

questions.question: Which of the following invasive weed species introduced into India has posed a serious environmental threat to native flora and human health?
questions.solution: Invasive weed species such as carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana, and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) cause environmental damage and pose threats to native Indian species.

questions.question: The illegal introduction of the African catfish ________ for aquaculture purposes is posing a major threat to the indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers:
questions.solution: The illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture purposes is posing a serious threat to native indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.

questions.question: Co-extinction is illustrated when:
options: A host fish species becomes extinct, causing the obligate parasitic parasites on it to also become extinct
Two predator species hunt each other to extinction
An invasive weed outcompetes a native crop
A bird migrates to another continent permanently
questions.solution: When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct. For example, when a host fish becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets extinction (co-extinction).

questions.question: Bioprospecting is defined as:
options: Exploring molecular, genetic, and species-level diversity for products of economic importance
Mining heavy metals from ocean beds
Extracting fossil fuels using transgenic bacteria
questions.solution: Bioprospecting refers to exploring molecular, genetic, and species-level diversity for products of economic importance (medicines, enzymes, agrochemicals).

questions.question: More than 25 percent of the drugs currently sold in the global pharmaceutical market are derived from plants, and approximately how many species of plants contribute to traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world?
questions.solution: More than 25 per cent of drugs in the market are derived from plants and around 25,000 species of plants contribute to traditional medicines used by native peoples worldwide.

questions.question: The Amazon rain forest is estimated to produce what percentage of the total oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere through photosynthesis (a broadly utilitarian ecological service)?
questions.solution: The broadly utilitarian argument says that biodiversity plays a major role in ecosystem services that nature provides. The Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.

questions.question: In-situ (on-site) conservation differs from Ex-situ (off-site) conservation because In-situ conservation involves:
options: Protecting and conserving endangered species in their entire natural ecosystem (e.g., National parks and Biosphere reserves)
Taking threatened animals out of their natural habitat and placing them in zoological parks
Preserving gametes in liquid nitrogen at $-196^\circ\text{C}$
Propagating plants through tissue culture in test tubes
questions.solution: In-situ conservation is the approach of protecting and conserving the whole ecosystem so that its biodiversity at all levels is protected (e.g., protecting the whole forest to save the tiger). Ex-situ involves taking threatened animals/plants out from their natural habitat into special settings (zoos, botanical gardens, cryobanks).

questions.question: Biodiversity Hotspots are regions characterized by:
options: Very high levels of species richness, high degree of endemism, and high level of habitat threat
Low species richness with no human interference
High concentration of alien species exclusively
Extensive cold desert vegetation with zero human habitation
questions.solution: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism (species confined to that region and not found anywhere else), and they are under severe threat of habitat destruction.

questions.question: Initially, 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified globally, but subsequent additions have brought the total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world to:
questions.solution: Initially 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified, but subsequently nine more have been added to the list, bringing the total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world to 34.

questions.question: Which of the following three biodiversity hotspots cover exceptionally high biodiversity regions of India?
options: Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya
Eastern Ghats, Thar Desert, and Gangetic Plain
Aravalli Hills, Deccan Plateau, and Sunderbans
Western Himalayas, Nilgiri, and Rann of Kutch only
questions.solution: Three of the global biodiversity hotspots—Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya—cover India's exceptionally high biodiversity regions.

questions.question: All the 34 biodiversity hotspots put together cover less than ________ percent of the Earth's land area, but strict protection of these hotspots could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost ________ percent:
questions.solution: Although all the biodiversity hotspots put together cover less than 2 per cent of the Earth's land area, the number of species they collectively harbor is extremely high, and strict protection of these hotspots could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.

questions.question: In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as:
options: 14 Biosphere Reserves, 90 National Parks, and 448 Wildlife Sanctuaries
50 Biosphere Reserves, 500 National Parks, and 100 Sanctuaries
34 Biosphere Reserves, 14 National Parks, and 90 Sanctuaries
4 Biosphere Reserves, 10 National Parks, and 50 Sanctuaries
questions.solution: According to NCERT data, India now has 14 Biosphere Reserves, 90 National Parks, and 448 Wildlife Sanctuaries for in-situ conservation.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the Sacred Groves of India and their geographical states:

List-I (Sacred Grove Location)List-II (Indian State / Region)
(A) Khasi and Jaintia Hills(I) Rajasthan
(B) Aravalli Hills(II) Meghalaya
(C) Western Ghat regions(III) Madhya Pradesh
(D) Chanda and Bastar areas(IV) Karnataka and Maharashtra

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Khasi and Jaintia Hills: Meghalaya; Aravalli Hills: Rajasthan; Western Ghat regions: Karnataka and Maharashtra; Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas: Madhya Pradesh/Chhattisgarh. In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.

questions.question: Sacred groves are highly revered tracts of forest where:
options: All trees and wildlife are venerated and given total community protection due to cultural and religious traditions
Commercial timber logging is legally permitted by tribal chiefs
Ex-situ cryobanks are maintained by local universities
questions.solution: Sacred groves are undisturbed forest patches held sacred by local communities based on cultural and religious beliefs, providing total protection to all native plants and wildlife.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an EX-SITU (off-site) conservation method?
options: Zoological parks, Botanical gardens, and Cryopreservation of gametes
questions.solution: Ex-situ conservation methods involve taking threatened species out of their natural habitats and caring for them in human-controlled settings (Zoological parks, Botanical gardens, Wildlife safari parks, seed banks, cryopreservation, and in vitro tissue culture).

questions.question: Cryopreservation of gametes of threatened species in a viable and fertile condition for long periods is carried out using liquid nitrogen at what temperature?
questions.solution: Gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques in liquid nitrogen at $-196^\circ\text{C}$.

questions.question: The historic Convention on Biological Diversity ('The Earth Summit') held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 called upon all nations to:
options: Take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilization of its benefits
Ban the commercial use of all synthetic fertilizers worldwide
Impose total trade embargoes on plastic production
questions.solution: The historic Convention on Biological Diversity ('The Earth Summit') held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for the conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilization of its benefits.

questions.question: The World Summit on Sustainable Development was held in 2002 in which city and country?
questions.solution: The World Summit on Sustainable Development was held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa, where 190 countries pledged their commitment to achieve a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.

questions.question: According to the IUCN Red List, what percentage of all bird species, mammal species, amphibian species, and gymnosperm species currently face the threat of extinction globally?
questions.solution: Presently, 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species, and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species in the world face the threat of extinction. Amphibians appear to be the most vulnerable.

questions.question: Which of the following vertebrate groups is considered the MOST vulnerable to extinction, with 32 percent of its global species threatened?
questions.solution: Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrate group, with 32 per cent of all amphibian species facing the threat of extinction due to their delicate moist skin, habitat fragmentation, and fungal infections.

questions.question: Endemism is defined as:
options: Species confined to a specific geographical region and not found anywhere else
Species distributed uniformly across all continents
Species introduced into a non-native habitat from outside
Species that breed only once in their lifetime
questions.solution: Endemism refers to species that are confined strictly to a particular geographic region and are not found naturally anywhere else on Earth.

questions.question: The Red Data Book (or IUCN Red List) maintained by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) contains a catalogue of:
options: Taxa facing the risk of global extinction (critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable)
All economically valuable cultivated crop varieties
Genetically modified microorganisms approved for release
Exotic invasive species introduced in agricultural lands
questions.solution: The Red Data Book / IUCN Red List maintains a comprehensive catalogue and assessment of the global conservation status of biological species facing high risks of extinction.

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding the ethical argument for conserving biodiversity:
Statement I: We share this planet with millions of plant, animal, and microbial species, and every species has an intrinsic value even if it is of no direct economic value to us.
Statement II: We have a moral duty to care for their well-being and pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are correct according to NCERT. The ethical argument for conserving biodiversity relates to what we owe to millions of plant, animal, and microbe species with whom we share this planet; philosophically or spiritually, each species has an intrinsic value.

questions.question: Which of the following is an in-situ conservation zone where no human activity (such as forestry, grazing, or cultivation) is permitted whatsoever?
questions.solution: A National Park is an in-situ conservation area strictly reserved for the protection of wildlife and biodiversity where activities like grazing, forestry, habitat destruction, and private ownership are strictly prohibited.

questions.question:
Read the following statements regarding species diversity:
Statement I: Fungi have more species than all the vertebrate species combined (fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals).
Statement II: Prokaryotic species diversity cannot be accurately estimated using conventional taxonomic methods.

Choose the correct option:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution: Both statements are correct according to NCERT. The number of fungal species in the world is more than the combined total of the species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals. Conventional taxonomic methods are unsuitable for identifying microbes, and many prokaryotic species cannot be cultured in laboratory media, making their true diversity difficult to estimate without biochemical/molecular tools.
